doc.title: Ray Shiner interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 11, 1998

title: Union dealings: recording line, fees and transfer
summary: Contracts approved by the union, picking up checks, initiation fee, six-month wait for Local 802 card, and Three Penny Opera.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: And all this stuff was tied in to the union too, right?
The union was there because we had to belong to the union.
Yeah. And so when you went to do a date—
Of course the union collected all the money, because we had to hand in contracts, and they had to be approved by the union.
And then you had to go to the union office to get your pay, is that right?

Yes. I’d get in line, they had a recording line, people who would direct the dates, you’d go up to the date and you’d tell Julie your name, and he’d look on the list and say, “You’ve got three checks” or, “you don’t have any checks today.” You know, so he would tell you, and give you the checks and you’d pay your union tax and that was it. © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-
What did it cost to belong to the local in the early 50s? Do you recall?
I think it cost $52 for an initiation fee, maybe $25 a year dues. It’s much more than that now.
And you had, was there like a six month period or something—

I had a six month period and I had to transfer, I transferred from the Rochester local which was my home local. It took six months. And you could do casuals, you could single dates, which I did, and that sustained me while I was waiting for the 802. And then when I got the 802, the New York Union Card, then I could take a steady job. And then I took a steady job that paid $85 a week, which was nothing. I did the original “Three Penny Opera” down in the Villages with Lottie Lenya and Bea Arthur. Oh you should have seen who was on the cast. Leon Janney, some famous people, Jerry Stiller from Stiller & Meara, and Jerry Orbach was in the show, and Bea Arthur. Some really famous names on Broadway. That was their first gig. We all did “Three Penny Opera” for scale. I have to tell you a funny thing that happened. Charlie Russo was the other sax player and we were in full view of the audience and I played tenor sax and clarinet. And at one point there was a tenor sax solo in the dark. And I played the solo. And in the middle of the solo I let out a squeak that you wouldn’t believe, unintentionally naturally. And the lights went on and my face was red, and Charlie Russo reaches in his pocket, in full view of the audience, and puts a band-aid on my stand and says, “Are you okay?” So you know, a sense a humor sustains you.
